source.title: An Evidence-Based and Mechanistic Approach to Reducing the Risk of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: An Exercise and Sport Science Australia Position Statement

paper.citation: Collings TJ, Diamond LE, Barrett RS, Saxby DJ, Lloyd DG, Whiteley R, Patterson BE, Crossley KM, Bourne MN. An Evidence-Based and Mechanistic Approach to Reducing the Risk of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: An Exercise and Sport Science Australia Position Statement. Sports Medicine. 2026. doi:10.1007/s40279-026-02450-3.
paper.abstract: This Exercise and Sport Science Australia position statement combined two systematic searches with mechanistic evidence to evaluate exercise-based ACL injury-risk reduction and propose a tiered prescription framework. Tier 1 comprises population-level multicomponent neuromuscular or structured warm-up programs. Tier 2 comprises targeted movement, strength, feedback, and neurocognitive strategies whose mechanistic rationale currently exceeds their direct injury-incidence evidence.
paper.tldr: Multicomponent neuromuscular and structured warm-up programs have the strongest evidence for reducing ACL injury incidence, particularly in adolescent female soccer, basketball, and handball. Individualized biomechanical or neurocognitive strategies may be useful adjuncts, but they have not yet demonstrated reduced ACL injury incidence.
paper.methods: The authors searched Scopus, Embase, and PubMed. One search identified controlled and cohort studies evaluating exercise interventions against ACL injury incidence; a second identified prospective intrinsic risk-factor studies. They integrated those findings with video, in vivo, in vitro, and in silico biomechanical evidence to develop a two-tier exercise framework.
paper.findings: Meta-analyses summarized by the statement estimate an approximately 60% reduction in ACL injury risk from multicomponent programs in female soccer, basketball, or handball players aged 14–18 years. Effective programs commonly included plyometric, bodyweight-strength, balance or proprioception, mobility, and agility elements for 10–30 minutes, two to three times weekly. Higher adherence was associated with greater effectiveness. Direct injury-incidence evidence for targeted Tier 2 strategies remains limited.
paper.limitations: The strongest intervention evidence is concentrated in adolescent female cutting and landing sports. Evidence in males, elite athletes, American football, and several other sports is limited. The statement combines multiple evidence types with different inferential strength, and modifiable biomechanical associations do not by themselves establish causal injury mechanisms or prevention effects.
paper.practicalImplications: Prioritize a sustainable multicomponent Tier 1 program, monitor delivery and adherence, and adapt implementation to the sport and training environment. Add targeted Tier 2 work only for a clearly defined athlete need and describe it as an adjunct with mechanistic support rather than as a proven way to reduce ACL injuries.
paper.athleteDev: Build landing, deceleration, strength, balance, and agility exposure progressively within normal training. Preserve individual coaching and movement assessment, but do not convert a screening score or movement pattern into a deterministic injury label.
paper.rtp: This statement addresses primary injury-risk reduction rather than return-to-play clearance. Its exercise categories may inform late-stage reconditioning after ACL injury, but it provides no validated clearance threshold, reinjury prediction rule, or sport-specific return progression.
